text: the world. The major risk factor for these cancers is the use of tobacco (whether chewed, inhaled, or smoked). Alcohol acts synergistically with tobacco to increase the risk. Hu- man papillomavirus infection appears to be a risk factor for some squamous cancers of the oropharynx. Endemic na- sopharyngeal cancer in parts of India, China, and North Africa is associated with Epstein-Barr virus and the con- sumption of salt-cured fish. Premalignant lesions include leucoplakia and erythropla- kia, and these can progress to invasive cancer. About one- third of cancers are diagnosed at early stages (I and II), and the rest are usually locally advanced (stage III and IVA). Although early-stage disease can be successfully treated, there is a high incidence of second primary cancers in the head and neck, lung, or oesophagus. Therefore, there is in- terest in the development of chemopreventive drugs to re- duce this risk. Fewer than 30% of patients with locally ad- vanced disease are cured. The treatment of head and neck cancer is complex, and is affected by the site and extent of disease, pathological findings, lymph node involvement, the patient’s functional status, and comorbidities; the expe- rience and skill of the team carrying out surgery and radi- otherapy will also influence treatment recommendations.1 In early-stage resectable cancers, such as those of the oral cavity and oropharynx, surgery or radiotherapy (external beam irradiation or brachytherapy) are the mainstays of treatment.1,2 Postoperative chemoradiotherapy may be used when extracapsular nodal spread or positive margins are found.1 For anatomically unresectable early-stage dis- ease, such as in the nasopharynx, radiotherapy alone is generally used, but primary chemoradiotherapy should be considered for patients with adverse prognostic factors such as nodal spread.1 Locally advanced disease is usually treated with combina- tion therapy. Resectable disease is managed with surgery and adjuvant radiotherapy.1 The addition of chemotherapy has been studied in resectable disease, but induction chem- otherapy (given before surgery and radiotherapy) has not been found to consistently improve survival rates.3 Post- operative chemoradiotherapy has produced inconsistent results, and there is insufficient evidence that it has any ad- vantage over adjuvant radiotherapy.3 In unresectable local- ly advanced disease, and in resectable disease when the aim is to avoid the need for surgery and thereby allow or- gan preservation, chemotherapy with radiotherapy is gen- erally used, and different regimens have been tried.
